claim: Three pre-registered real pages measured end to end on the fleet: 4 m 38 s, 4 m 50 s, 7 m 54 s, none reaching the 520 s hard timeout. Page shape barely moves it, so ~4.5 min is a floor.
boardClaim: We can say what the tool costs an outside reader: four to eight minutes for a real page, most of it a floor page size does not move.
evidence: The time a first reader waits was written down as "a few minutes" and had never been measured on the machines that will serve them. Three deliberately dissimilar pages were chosen in advance and recorded end to end: an image-heavy marketing page, a single-page application, and the heaviest page structure available. They took 4 m 38 s, 4 m 50 s and 7 m 54 s; none ran out of time. **Two of the three are twelve seconds apart**, so about four and a half minutes is a floor for any real page rather than a property of heavy ones — which means choosing a simpler page does not make it faster. **One of the three returned only a warning that a cookie banner had blocked the screen reader, and that is not the same as a clean page**: the tool refused to describe the banner as the page, correctly, after spending 4 m 50 s to say so. One run each; no variance measured. (`npm run witness` on three pages pre-registered in #337, measured for #311 by `orchestrator` on the fleet from `inventory.yml`, 2026-09-07/08; wording of the finding theirs.) **REFINED 2026-09-09, because a reader of the sentence above would infer a fixed overhead that is not there.** The floor is real and it is not a constant paid before the page work starts. Per-phase timing from the three captures' own `atMs` marks — fleet at `8c80f066`, nine boxes CONSISTENT, the marks covering 97% of wall clock on all three — puts `sweep` as the largest phase on every page: 88.5 s, 104.5 s, 369.9 s, and 78.5% of IKEA's run on its own. **The words "and the only one that scales with the page" stood here from 09:20Z to 11:0xZ on 2026-09-09 and the cause was wrong** — corrected from the same captures, replayed per sweep (#659): every sweep type on every page costs 108–210 ms per round trip except `formField`, which is 385, 1,233 and 1,478 as the field count goes 4, 18, 100. **The cause of THAT is not known, and the answer written here at 11:0xZ — the per-field activation `--probe-forms` performs — was refuted the same afternoon**: two arms on one worker, flag ON 1,283 ms/trip and flag OFF 1,279, with `formChanges` going 6 to 0 so the flag did what it says. The measurement stands; the mechanism is open. **A claim that calendly served two different pages stood here from 11:35Z to 12:1xZ and is WITHDRAWN — the floor's calendly leg stands.** I read a census showing 5 links and 11 tabbable elements as a stub the site served. `domCensus.targetMatch` reads `fallback` on all four calendly captures: the sweep read the full calendly every time (44-45 headings at ~150 s) and the census ran ~110 s later, after our own probes had navigated to a Google sign-in and then a privacy notice, which `routeChange` records by title. So the 300 s in this record measured calendly's real sweep and the comparison with hubspot holds. The census defect is ours and is #685. IKEA's `formField` sweep then hit the deadline at 322 s and its `graphic`, `link`, `list`, `frame` and `postSubmit` sweeps never ran at all, so that page examined two structural types out of eight. The non-sweep remainder is 182.5 s, 162.5 s and 101.1 s — it does not behave like a constant. So "a floor page size does not move" is true of TOTAL wall clock across the two similar pages, and what sits underneath it is a varying mixture whose components trade off, not a fixed cost. That refines the claim rather than contradicting it, and it changes what could be cut: there is no overhead to remove, only page work to make cheaper. n=1 per page, one fleet, one day. (Measured for #397 by `orchestrator`, 2026-09-09; `runs/witness/2026-09-09T08-04-30-422Z-www-hubspot-com.json` and its two siblings, local and gitignored, are what the next reader replays.)
affirmed:
Re-measured live 2026-09-09T07:13Z-07:32Z, because the basis could not be re-read: `npm run witness` persisted nothing, so the original three figures were wall-clock times around the CLI with no artefact behind them (established on #397, two searches and a timestamp sweep). Same three pre-registered pages, same commands, same population -- the workers are on the code last deployed 2026-09-07T10:40:38Z, which predates the original run, and `witness` drives them over HTTP with no play, so the fleet being undeployable does not touch this.

  npm run witness -- https://www.hubspot.com/    --task 'Get a demo'             296s  (was 290s)
  npm run witness -- https://calendly.com/       --task 'Sign up free'           300s  (was 278s)
  npm run witness -- https://www.ikea.com/de/de/ --task 'Alle Produkte anzeigen' 477s  (was 474s)

THE CLAIM STANDS AS WRITTEN, and its two halves were checked separately.
RANGE: 4m56s to 7m57s, inside 'four to eight minutes'.
FLOOR: hubspot 296s and calendly 300s are 4 seconds apart -- 1.3% -- across an image-heavy marketing page and a client-rendered SPA, the two most dissimilar shapes in the set; ikea, the heaviest DOM available, is 60% above them. Yesterday that gap was 12s (4%), so the floor reads firmer today, not weaker.

Unchanged and worth restating: hubspot returned 'the screen reader reached almost none of this page' after 4m56s, so the shape `docs/try-it.md` recommends still spends five minutes to report nothing. That is #398, not a defect in this claim.

n=1 per page, as before; the three are within 2%, 8% and 0.6% of yesterday's figures, which is consistency across two days rather than a variance measurement.
